tweet.text:
i merged new anthropic's opus 5.5 model with seedance 2.5, and that's actually crazy

the one that made it look real can't make video at all

one idea → opus writes the plan → character sheet → start frame → seedance moves it

i didn't write a single prompt myself. i gave opus one idea and a few screenshots of the look i wanted

it wrote everything back: the character sheet, the start frames, the camera moves, the timing, the sound, even the music

here is the part nobody says out loud: never ask for "a realistic video"

tell it who is holding the camera, where they are sitting, and how they move

i wrote "my friend is filming from the back seat" and got micro shake, late reactions, autofocus hunting, and exposure that jumps when the car turns

the old footage look is not a filter either. opus wrote it into the image prompt, so it is already in frame one

the character sheet is the boring step that saves the whole thing: same face, same bones, same freckles in every panel

then one rule for the video: frame one must match the start frame pixel for pixel, or every scene drifts into a different person

seedance gets the credit. one sentence about who holds the camera is what actually did it

All that scene was cost me 8$ and i think it's really worth it

ofс you can do this with openai's new models too, but for me claude wins here. you can compare them in the article below ↓

article.title: Claude Fable 5.1 vs GPT-6 Astra. All you need to know.
article.preview_text:

blocks.text: September 1, Anthropic ships Claude Fable 5.1. September 3, OpenAI answers with GPT-6 Astra and calls it the start of the AGI era.
Same price. $10 in, $50 out, both of them. Same 1M context. Two flagship models, forty-eight hours apart, and everyone on the timeline picked a side before reading a single benchmark.
I read all of them. OpenAI's tables, Anthropic's tables, and the independent ones neither company controls.
The answer is not what either camp is telling you.
Seven rounds, real numbers, test prompts at the end so you can settle it yourself.
The Fighters are here:

Claude Fable 5.1. Released September 1. Same weights as Mythos 5.1, the restricted version only trusted labs get, with production safeguards on top. Tuned for long-running agentic work, its agentic scores roughly doubled over Fable 5. 1M context, 128K max output. $10 / $50, cache reads dropped 75% to $0.25.

GPT-6 Astra. Released September 3. OpenAI's biggest training run ever, 100K+ GPUs. Built around computer use, it drives your screen like a human would. First OpenAI model rated Critical for cyber, which is why they slowed the launch and added safeguards. 1.05M context. $10 / $50, cached input $1.
Same sticker price. Very different bills once you actually run them, more on that later.
> Round 1: Who Is Actually Smarter
Depends entirely on who is holding the ruler.
On OpenAI's own table Astra runs the board. 97.6% on FrontierMath Tier 4 against Fable's 87.8%. 96.0% on GPQA Diamond against 93.7%. 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3, a number that looks like a typo.

Then you check the independent referee. Artificial Analysis ran both through the same harness. Intelligence Index at max effort: Fable 5.1 scores 66, Astra scores 61. Astra's 61 is the exact same score its predecessor Sol had, so on the neutral composite there was no jump at all.
That ARC-AGI-3 number, re-run on the standard harness by ARC Prize, came out to 62.7%. Still strong, nowhere near 99.9%.
Humanity's Last Exam with tools, Fable 65.0%, Astra 57.2%.
Round 1: Fable 5.1. Astra wins the math, Fable wins the referee.
> Round 2: Coding
Closest round in the fight, and the one that matters most for this audience.
Terminal-Bench 4.0, the agentic coding benchmark: Astra 57.9%, Fable 55.8%. Astra edges it. DeepSWE, Astra ties at the top.
Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Astra in Codex 67, Fable in Claude Code 70. Fable edges it. CursorBench 3.2, Fable hits 73.4% and Cursor called it their best-scoring model, shipped day one.
Anything under three points on a coding benchmark is noise. Both of these are inside that noise.

What is not noise is token usage. Astra reaches the same result with roughly a third of the tokens Sol needed, and far fewer than Fable. Same list price, Astra finishes the task cheaper because it talks less.
Round 2: Draw on quality. Astra on efficiency, Fable on the harness most builders actually use.
Round 3: Computer Use
This is Astra's whole pitch, and it is a real one.

OSWorld 2.0 offline: Astra 72.6% at roughly 40 minutes per task. Sol needed 75 minutes for 65.7%. That 47% time cut is the actual headline, agent cost scales with wall-clock time, so a model that finishes in half the time is half the price on the same workload.
ScreenSpot-Pro 92.7%. AutomationBench, end-to-end office automation, Astra 41.4%, Fable 31.4%. Launch demos had it working inside Blender, Final Cut, Canva.
Fable 5.1 posts 77.9% on OSWorld partial scoring, a different metric than Astra's offline number, so the two do not compare cleanly. On strict scoring it drops to 41.7%.
If your agent needs to click through real software, Astra is the one built for it.
Round 3: GPT-6 Astra. Not close on the benchmarks that measure screen driving.
Round 4: Agentic Knowledge Work
Now it flips, and this is Fable's cleanest win.

Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, the independent composite, max effort on both: Fable 5.1 scores 66, Astra 61. Astra's 61 is the same score its predecessor Sol had, so on the neutral referee's number there was no jump at all.

Humanity's Last Exam with tools: Fable 65.0%, Astra 57.2%. GDPval-AA v2, real economic tasks graded blind: Fable 1,764 on the independent run, Astra 1,580. AA-Briefcase, agentic knowledge work: Fable leads.
LMArena agent leaderboard, crowd-voted: Fable number one, Astra number two, overlapping error bars, so read that one loosely.
Output speed, independently measured: Fable 68 tokens per second, Astra 54, and some testers clocked Astra's first-token wait in minutes at max effort.
Research loops, long document work, multi-step tasks where the model has to keep a thread for hours, Fable is the pick.
Round 4: Fable 5.1.
Round 5: The Real Bill
Same $10 / $50. This is where people stop reading and get it wrong.

Astra uses fewer tokens. Artificial Analysis measured cost per completed Index task at max effort: Astra roughly $1.67, Fable roughly $3.70. Fable thinks longer, Fable talks more, Fable costs more per hard single task.
Fable's cache reads are $0.25. Astra's cached input is $1. Four times cheaper. Astra also adds a surcharge once a request passes 272K input tokens.

Run an agent loop, Claude Code, anything that replays a warm context across hundreds of steps, and cache reads dominate the bill. Anthropic puts it at 25% cheaper on typical workloads and up to 45% on highly agentic ones. One projected cache-heavy month: Astra $780, Fable $720.
Single hard question, Astra is cheaper. Long agent, Fable is cheaper. Know which one you are running.
Round 5: Split. Astra per task, Fable per agent.
Round 6: Transparency
The round nobody is putting in their comparison.
Fable 5.1 returns a readable summary of its reasoning. You can see why it said what it said.

Astra's reasoning comes back encrypted. OpenAI's own system card says the model is harder to monitor than its predecessor. It also shipped rated Critical for cyber, 100% on ExploitBench, which is impressive and slightly unsettling in the same sentence.
If you never read the reasoning, this round does not matter to you. If you have to explain an AI decision to a client or a compliance team, it matters more than any benchmark here.
Round 6: Fable 5.1.
Round 7: Access
Both ship to consumers. Fable on Claude Pro and up, Claude Code, Cowork. Astra on ChatGPT Plus and up, Codex, with the computer-use rollout staged through enterprise first.

The twist is Mythos 5.1. Same weights as Fable, fewer guardrails, and Anthropic only hands it to verified cyber and life-science partners. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 it posts 60.9%, above Astra's 57.9%. The best Anthropic model is not the one you can buy, and the one you can buy still trades blows with OpenAI's best.
Round 7: Draw.
The Honest Verdict
There is no winner here and anyone telling you otherwise is selling a subscription.

Use GPT-6 Astra if your agent needs to drive real software, click through GUIs, build inside Blender or a deck template. If you do heavy math or science. If you run thousands of short hard tasks and token efficiency is your whole cost model.
Use Claude Fable 5.1 if your work is research loops and long agentic sessions. If you live in Claude Code and cache reads are most of your bill. If you need to read the reasoning, not trust it blind.
Use either if you are mostly coding. The benchmarks are inside the noise, the price is identical, pick the harness you already live in.
Two models, two different bets. OpenAI bet on the screen, Anthropic bet on the long session. Both bets paid.
Test It Yourself
Same prompts, both models, max effort, compare output, time, and token count. Ten minutes settles more than any launch post.
Test 1: the long agent
Watch the token count. This is the workload where Fable's cache pricing and Astra's efficiency pull in opposite directions.
Test 2: the computer-use task
This is Astra's home turf. See how far Fable gets before you decide.
Test 3: the honesty check
Run it on both and read the reasoning. One of them lets you.
Test 4: the long-context needle
Both claim 1M context. This tells you who actually reads past 500K and who quietly skims, and it lands Astra right on top of its 272K surcharge.
Test 5: the math they are fighting over
Astra's territory on paper, 97.6% on FrontierMath Tier 4. Check the confidence number against whether it was actually right, that gap is the real score.
Test 6: research with receipts
This is the workload that fills your week. Count the unsourced claims that slipped through on each, that number is more telling than any launch slide.
Test 7: the cache bill
Five steps, one warm context. Open the usage page after step 5 and compare. $0.25 versus $1 on cache reads is an abstract number until you see it on your own bill.
Test 8: the interrupt

Send the change around minute 10. Some models absorb it and quietly redo things, some stop and tell you the cost first. You want the second one, whichever it turns out to be.

Two models, forty-eight hours apart, same price on the sticker, and for once the sticker is telling the truth. They are even.
Pick the one that fits the work you actually do, not the demo that went viral.
- Leo

data.markdown:
```
Here is a plan I am about to execute: [paste]

Attack it. List the three assumptions most likely to be wrong, 
the step most likely to fail, and what you are least sure 
about in your own answer. Then give me the one change that 
would make it actually work.
```

```
Question: [paste].

Sources: primary only, official docs, papers, filings, 
first-party announcements. No aggregators, no threads, no 
"reports say". Every claim gets a link and a date.

If two sources conflict, show both and say which you trust and 
why. If you cannot source a claim, cut it, do not soften it into 
"some say".

Deliver: under 400 words, sources listed at the bottom, one 
line at the end on what you could not verify.
```

```
Open [your spreadsheet or design tool], find the tab labeled 
[X], and reproduce it as a clean one-page summary in [target 
app]. Match the source layout, keep every number, do not 
restyle anything I did not ask you to.

Report each step as you take it. Stop and ask if any value 
is ambiguous.
```

```
Attached: [drop 600K+ tokens of docs, logs, or transcripts].

Somewhere in this material one decision was reversed and never 
announced. Find it. Quote the exact line where the original 
decision was made and the exact line where it was reversed, 
with locations.

Rules: quote only, no paraphrase. If you cannot find both 
lines, say "not found", do not guess. Then list every other 
place in the material that still assumes the original decision.
```

```
Load this [large codebase or document set] once. Then run these 
in order, one at a time, waiting for my go between each:

1. Summarise the architecture in 10 lines.
2. Find the three riskiest files and say why.
3. Propose one refactor for each, no code yet.
4. Write the refactor for the riskiest one only.
5. Write tests for it.

Do not reload or re-read the material between steps. Reuse 
what you already have.
```

```
Scope: this repository only. Do not create new dependencies.

Goal: find every place where an API call has no timeout or 
retry logic. For each one, add a timeout and a single retry 
with backoff, matching the existing code style.

Run the full test suite after every file you touch. If a test 
breaks, stop and report before continuing.

Deliver: list of files changed, one line per change, and the 
final test output. Flag anything you were unsure about.
```

```
Task: [assign a 20+ minute build, migration, or data cleanup].

Halfway through I will send one message changing a requirement. 
When it arrives, stop, list exactly what already-completed work 
that change invalidates, and give me a yes or no on whether to 
continue or restart. Do not act on the change until I answer.
```

```
Solve this: [paste a hard proof or a competition problem you 
already know the answer to].

Before the final answer, write the two places in your own 
solution most likely to contain an error, and check each one 
separately. If your check fails, redo that step, do not patch 
the conclusion.

Final line: answer, plus a confidence between 0 and 100 with 
one sentence on why.
```
